source.title: Learned feature representations are biased by complexity, learning order, position, and more
source.authors: Andrew Kyle Lampinen; Stephanie C Y Chan; Katherine L. Hermann

record.file_problem: None; the full paper text, including supplemental analyses, is supplied.
record.tranche_reason: The paper studies representation biases in controlled tasks and discusses interpretability implications, but it does not test neuron-pole job counts, explanation validation on held-out activations, automated neuron-explanation scores, or attribution graphs.
record.gate_note: The paper reports controlled feature-representation results, including a qualitative per-unit analysis in a toy MLP. That analysis measures feature-related variance in individual units, not whether a neuron pole has one nameable job or what share of poles are interpretable. Its cited neuron-explanation work is not a result of this study.
record.test_reason: The study measures how much representation variance features explain in toy MLPs, transformers and CNNs trained on synthetic tasks. It does not count neuron poles by number of jobs, test neuron explanations against held-out activations, score explanations by simulation, examine InceptionV1 neurons, or build neuron attribution graphs. Its single per-unit analysis (Appendix B.4) reports feature-attributed variance per unit in one toy MLP run. That is a related but different construct from whether a neuron has one nameable job, so it goes under fits_no_version. The interpretability discussion is argument about variance-based methods, not a result on any version.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. The authors find that learned representations are biased toward or away from features by complexity, learning order, prevalence, output position and number of output values, with complex interactions with architecture, optimizer and dropout. They argue these biases can mislead variance-based interpretability methods such as PCA, SAEs and RSA, since low-variance features may still matter computationally.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses controlled feature tasks and linear regressions to measure representation variance, rather than auditing neuron-pole explanations or testing those explanations on activations.
record.method_sensitivity: The paper reports that representation biases can vary or even reverse with architecture, optimizer, dropout, feature order, feature position, and other task choices.

fits_no_version.finding: In one toy MLP run, most penultimate units carried more variance from the easy feature. Only a subset acquired hard-feature signal. Many units also carried non-trivial signal about other inputs.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In small MLPs trained on multiple synthetic features, individual units' feature-attributed variance is mixed and skewed toward simpler, earlier-learned features. This is a per-unit variance measure, not a count of single-job neurons.

record.problems: The authors note that the work uses simple synthetic datasets and toy-scale models, and that its main analyses rely on linear regression, which can miss information encoded nonlinearly or in superposition. The per-unit result recorded here is from a single run.
record.rows_left_out: No directly claim-testing results were omitted. The paper's other aggregate feature-variance, causal-intervention, and architecture results do not measure the neuron-pole job counts or explanation-validation outcomes named by the claim versions.

untested.parts: No audit of Qwen3-32B or of neuron poles by number of jobs.
No cross-model or cross-scale shares of interpretable neurons; only toy-scale synthetic models.
No InceptionV1 cat-and-car neuron, pose, or recursive generalization versus superposition analysis.
Architecture and optimizer comparisons concern feature-variance biases, not the share of interpretable neurons or tool quality.
No attribution graphs from neurons, replacement models, or reconstruction error.
No test of explanations from activating examples against where neurons fire.
No simulation-based scoring of neuron explanations.

record.verdict_notes: The paper cites Bills et al. 2023 (an original source) only in passing, among interpretability work that prioritizes high-variance features. It provides no result on neuron-explanation scores. Its sparsity analysis (Appendix B.5, Fig. 24) finds harder features are encoded more sparsely across units. That is also a related construct, not a version test.

versions.untested_parts: Does not audit Qwen3-32B or count neuron poles by number of jobs or understanding.
Does not compare neuron-pole interpretability shares across language models, dense and mixture-of-experts models, or scales up to trillions of parameters.
Does not examine InceptionV1 cat-and-car neurons, pose, or recursive generalization versus superposition.
Although it compares architectures and reports representation biases, it does not estimate the share of interpretable neurons or test the stated InceptionV1-sized estimates or tools claim.
Does not test attribution graphs built from a large model's own neurons or compare them with replacement models and reconstruction error.
Does not test explanations against activating examples or measure whether they predict where neurons fire.
Does not score neuron explanations by simulating activations on new text.

rows.subject: 4-layer MLP (basic model)
rows.stage_stated: end of training and selected training stages
rows.operation_detail: Analyzed feature-attributed variance for individual penultimate-layer units.

conditions.value: linear easy feature and sum-mod-2 hard feature

rows.measure: Per-unit representation variance attributed to features
rows.value: The authors report that most units continued to carry more variance due to the easy feature. Only a subset of initially easy-selective units later acquired some hard-feature signal; a few units that initially carried at least as much signal about the hard inputs as about the easy ones became somewhat more selective for the hard inputs.
rows.note: This is a qualitative per-unit feature-variance result from a toy MLP, not a count of neurons with one or multiple jobs, and it does not assess explanation quality.
rows.check: Link to none and state are correct. The row is from a single run of a 4-layer toy MLP (64 penultimate units). It measures per-unit variance attributed to trained features, not neuron-pole job counts or explanation quality. Subject, condition and locator match Appendix B.4. The value text is accurate. The text also notes many units carry non-trivial signal about other inputs.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.
